prompt: An element has `width: 200px`, `padding: 20px` and `border: 2px`. How much horizontal space does it occupy, in CSS's default behaviour?
hint: By default, `width` measures only one of the box's four layers. Which one — and do the others go inwards or outwards?

choices.text: 244px, because by default `width` measures only the content and padding and border add outwards.
200px, because `width` always sets the element's final width on screen.
choices.why: That becomes true with `border-box`, which is not the default.

choices.text: 240px, because the border is drawn over the padding and adds no width.
choices.why: The border takes up space of its own, between padding and margin.

choices.text: 204px, because the padding is inside the content and does not add up.
choices.why: Padding is inside the box, but outside the content — and it adds up by default.

prompt: Tick the true statements about units.
hint: One of them is the reason text sized in pixels is an accessibility problem. Another concerns a unit that compounds when elements nest.

choices.text: `rem` respects whoever enlarged the default font in the browser; `px` ignores that preference.
choices.why: It is why typography is measured in `rem`.

choices.text: `em` compounds in nested elements, because it is relative to the element's own font size.
choices.why: Two levels of `1.2em` give 1.44 times the size, not 1.2.

choices.text: On a phone, `svh` and `dvh` cope better than `vh` with the browser bar appearing and disappearing.
choices.why: `vh` pins the height to the larger window and leaves content hidden behind the bar.

choices.text: `%` is always relative to the size of the window.
choices.why: `%` is relative to the container; the ones referring to the window are `vw`/`vh`.

choices.text: `box-sizing: border-box` changes the meaning of `margin` as well as `width`.
choices.why: Margin is outside the box and is unaffected; what changes is what `width` and `height` measure.
